title: “IF GOD IS FOR US, WHO CAN BE AGAINST US?” — THEN WHY DID PAUL IMMEDIATELY LIST EVERYTHING THAT CAME AGAINST CHRISTIANS?
paragraphs: “IF GOD IS FOR US, WHO CAN BE AGAINST US?” — THEN WHY DID PAUL IMMEDIATELY LIST EVERYTHING THAT CAME AGAINST CHRISTIANS?
The verse we quote when we want victory was written by a man who knew suffering. And what Paul actually meant may change the way you understand every battle you are fighting.
There is something almost heartbreaking about the way Christians sometimes quote Romans 8:31.
“If God be for us, who can be against us?”
We say it when we need courage. We post it when somebody betrays us. We whisper it before walking into situations that terrify us.
And there is nothing wrong with that.
But there is something deeply unsettling about what happens when you keep reading.
Because the very same apostle who declared that God was for us immediately began talking about trouble, persecution, hunger, nakedness, danger, and even death.
Wait.
If God is for us, why are His people still suffering?
If God is for us, why do faithful Christians still get sick?
Why do people who pray still lose loved ones?
Why do believers who refuse to compromise sometimes lose their jobs, their friendships, their reputations, and everything they worked so hard to build?
Why does the mother who has spent years praying for her children sometimes cry herself to sleep?
Why does the man who finally surrendered his life to Jesus discover that following Christ has not made his battles disappear?
And why do some of the people who love God most seem to carry wounds that nobody else can see?
Maybe you have wondered about this.
Maybe you have been afraid to say it out loud.
Because somewhere along the way, you heard that strong faith means you should always be victorious, always smiling, always confident, always expecting everything to work out exactly as you prayed.
And when it didn't...
You wondered whether something was wrong with your faith.
But what if the problem was never that you believed God's promise too much?
What if you were taught to expect something God never promised?
Stay with me.
Because the truth hidden in the surrounding verses of Romans 8 is not weaker than the promise you have been quoting.
It is infinitely more powerful.
And it begins with a man who understood what it meant to be opposed.
His name was Paul.
Before he became an apostle, he was a persecutor.
Before he wrote about the security of God's love, he had participated in the terror experienced by people who followed Jesus.
Acts 8:3 describes Saul ravaging the church, entering houses, and dragging believers away to prison.
Imagine the sound of frightened footsteps.
Imagine a Christian family hearing someone approaching their door.
Imagine a mother pulling her children closer because the name of Jesus had become dangerous to confess publicly.
And imagine the man responsible for some of that fear.
Saul.
The future Paul.
A man with religious credentials, strong convictions, and a terrible misunderstanding of God.
He believed he was defending the truth while persecuting people who belonged to the Truth Himself.
Then Jesus confronted him on the road to Damascus.
“Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?” (Acts 9:4, KJV).
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not merely ask why Saul was persecuting Christians.
He said, “Why persecutest thou me?”
The risen Christ so identified Himself with His people that their persecution was an offense against Him.
Think about that for a moment.
The people Saul dragged away were not abandoned by Jesus.
Their suffering mattered to Jesus.
And the persecutor himself would become living evidence that even a deeply guilty life could be rewritten by grace.
The man who once terrorized the church would eventually suffer for the gospel he had tried to destroy.
The man who once helped make believers afraid would become the man who wrote:
“If God be for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31, KJV).
But Paul was not writing from a life untouched by pain.
He knew what opposition looked like.
In 2 Corinthians 11:23–27, he recounts imprisonments, beatings, dangers, sleepless nights, hunger, thirst, cold, and exposure.
This was not a man selling the illusion that faith makes life comfortable.
This was a man who had discovered that Christ can remain faithful even when life becomes unbearable.
And now we arrive at the question so many people misunderstand.
Romans 8:31 in Greek reads:
“Εἰ ὁ θεὸς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, τίς καθ’ ἡμῶν;”
Ei ho Theos hyper hēmōn, tis kath’ hēmōn?
Literally:
“If God is for us, who is against us?”
The Greek expression ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν (hyper hēmōn) means “for us” or “on our behalf.”
And καθ’ ἡμῶν (kath’ hēmōn) expresses opposition against us.
But Paul is not suggesting that nobody will ever oppose Christians.
How could he?
He had experienced too much opposition to believe that.
Instead, he is asking a rhetorical question whose answer depends on the entire argument of Romans 8.
Who can successfully stand against those whom God has determined to save through Jesus Christ?
Who can overturn God's ultimate purpose?
Who can make the sacrifice of Jesus insufficient?
Who can bring a charge that defeats God's justification?
Who can separate believers from the love of Christ?
Paul's answer is not that enemies will never appear.
His answer is that no enemy can finally defeat God's saving purpose for those who belong to Christ.
That distinction changes everything.
Because some of us have spent years measuring God's presence by the absence of problems.
When the bills were paid, we believed He was with us.
When the doctor gave good news, we believed He was with us.
When the relationship was peaceful, we believed He was with us.
But when the diagnosis changed...
When the marriage became painful...
When the person we trusted betrayed us...
When we prayed and heaven seemed silent...
Suddenly, we began wondering whether God had moved away.
And here is where Paul's words become painfully personal.
Romans 8:35 asks:
“Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?” (KJV).
Read that again.
Paul did not say Christians would never experience tribulation.
He named it.
He did not say believers would never suffer distress.
He included it.
He did not promise that persecution would disappear, that hunger would never come, or that danger could never reach God's people.
He placed all those things directly inside his discussion of Christ's love.
Why?
Because the presence of suffering is not proof of the absence of God.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs that truth more than another motivational promise.
You have been faithful, but you are tired.
You have prayed, but you are still waiting.
You have forgiven, but the memories still hurt.
You have tried to rebuild your life, but some mornings you wake up feeling as though you are standing in the ruins all over again.
And the question you are almost ashamed to ask is:
“Lord, if You are for me, why is all this still against me?”
Paul does not answer by pretending the pain is imaginary.
He takes us somewhere much deeper.
He takes us to the cross.
Romans 8:32 says:
“He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?” (KJV).
Do you see what Paul is doing?
He is not telling suffering Christians to look at their circumstances and pretend everything is wonderful.
He is telling them to look at what God has already done in Jesus Christ.
The Father did not spare His own Son.
Jesus was betrayed.
Jesus was falsely accused.
Jesus was mocked.
Jesus was beaten.
Jesus was crucified.
And the people watching Him die could have looked at that cross and asked the very same question:
“If God is for Him, why is all this happening to Him?”
That is the scandal at the center of Christianity.
The sinless Son of God suffered.
The One who perfectly obeyed the Father was rejected by men.
The One who had power to calm storms submitted Himself to the cross.
And yet the cross was not proof that God's redemptive purpose had failed.
It was the very place where that purpose was being accomplished.
Jesus died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, as Paul declares in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
The resurrection vindicated the crucified Christ.
And through His death and resurrection, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are proclaimed to sinners who could never save themselves.
The darkest day in human history became the place where God's redeeming love was displayed.
That does not mean every tragedy in your life is secretly good.
Evil is still evil.
Death is still an enemy.
Abuse is still wrong.
Betrayal is still betrayal.
And the Bible never commands you to call darkness light.
But the cross proves that suffering and God's saving purpose are not necessarily contradictions.
The God who raised Jesus from the dead is not helpless before the things that frighten you.
And Paul goes even further.
Romans 8:33–34 asks who can bring a charge against God's elect and who can condemn them.
His answer rests in God's justifying work and in Jesus Christ, who died, rose again, is at God's right hand, and intercedes for His people.
That means the believer's ultimate security does not rest on having an impressive religious record.
It rests on Jesus.
Not on how beautifully you prayed yesterday.
Not on how confidently you spoke during worship.
Not on whether you managed to hide every tear.
Not on whether your past looks respectable enough for the people sitting beside you in church.
Jesus Christ is the Savior.
And this is where the gospel becomes almost unbearable in its beauty.
Because some of you are not merely fighting problems around you.
You are fighting memories within you.
You remember the things you did.
The people you hurt.
The promises you broke.
The sins you tried to justify.
The secret compromises nobody knows about.
The moments when you knew what was right and deliberately chose something else.
And perhaps you have wondered whether a person with your history could ever truly be welcomed by a holy God.
Paul's own story answers that question with extraordinary force.
The persecutor became a preacher of the Christ he had opposed.
Not because persecution was a small sin.
Not because his religious sincerity excused his actions.
But because the mercy of Jesus Christ is greater than the guilt of repentant sinners.
Paul wrote in 1 Timothy 1:15:
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.” (KJV).
He did not erase the truth about his past.
He magnified the mercy that met him there.
It is not about pretending the scandal never happened.
It is not about celebrating sin.
It is not about using grace as permission to continue in rebellion.
Romans 6:1–2 rejects that idea.
Grace does not make repentance unnecessary.
Grace brings sinners to the Savior who forgives and transforms.
It is about a guilty person being confronted by holy love.
A hardened heart being brought to repentance.
A broken life being surrendered to Jesus.
A sinner who once ran from God learning to walk with Him.
Not because the past was harmless.
But because the crucified and risen Christ is mighty to save.
And now Paul takes the argument into territory that should silence every shallow promise that Christians will always live comfortable lives.
Romans 8:36 says:
“As it is written, For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter.” (KJV).
Paul is quoting Psalm 44:22.
The Hebrew includes these words:
“כִּי־עָלֶיךָ הֹרַגְנוּ כָל־הַיּוֹם”
Ki ʿalekha horagnu khol-hayyom.
A close translation is:
“Yet for your sake we are killed all the day.”
This is not the language of people who believe faith makes them untouchable.
It is the cry of God's people suffering while still identifying themselves with Him.
Psalm 44 is a communal lament. The psalmist wrestles with the painful experience of suffering despite the people's appeal to their covenant faithfulness.
And Paul brings that ancient cry directly into his discussion of Christian suffering.
He knows that God's people can be afflicted without being abandoned.
He knows that devotion to God does not guarantee protection from every earthly danger.
And he knows that the ultimate hope of Christians must reach beyond physical survival.
Because then comes Romans 8:37.
“Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us.” (KJV).
Not away from all these things.
Not after every painful thing has disappeared.
In all these things.
The Greek word translated “more than conquerors” is:
“ὑπερνικῶμεν” — hypernikōmen.
It comes from a verb expressing decisive victory or prevailing overwhelmingly.
But notice something essential.
Paul says we are more than conquerors “through him that loved us.”
The victory is not self-generated.
It does not come from pretending to be invincible.
It does not mean every Christian will escape imprisonment, illness, poverty, or martyrdom.
It is victory grounded in Christ's love and His final saving triumph.
Paul is not offering a guarantee that believers will win every earthly battle.
He is proclaiming that no earthly battle can cancel the ultimate victory secured by Jesus Christ.
Some Christians were killed.
Some were imprisoned.
Some were rejected.
Some lost everything.
Yet even death could not make Christ's love powerless.
That is a far stronger promise than the assurance of an easy life.
And perhaps it is exactly the promise you need.
Because maybe your prayers have not produced the outcome you expected.
Maybe you have been asking God to restore something that has not been restored.
Maybe the person you wanted to reconcile with still refuses to speak to you.
Maybe the grief you carry has not disappeared.
Maybe you are doing your best to obey Jesus while living through circumstances you would never have chosen.
And you have quietly wondered:
“Am I losing?”
Listen carefully.
Your suffering does not automatically mean you are spiritually defeated.
Your tears do not mean your faith is counterfeit.
Your weakness does not mean Christ has stopped loving you.
And your unanswered questions do not mean you are forbidden to come to Him.
Even Paul pleaded with the Lord concerning his thorn in the flesh.
In 2 Corinthians 12:9, the Lord's answer included these words:
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.” (KJV).
God did not answer Paul's plea by making Paul independent of grace.
He taught Paul to depend on it.
And perhaps the deepest transformation in your life will not be that you become a person who never feels weak.
Perhaps it will be that you become a person who knows where to go with your weakness.
To Jesus.
Not to religious performance.
Not to manufactured positivity.
Not to the exhausting pressure of appearing victorious before everybody else.
To Jesus.
The One who receives repentant sinners.
The One who understands suffering.
The One who intercedes for His people.
The One who conquered death.
And the One whose love does not collapse when your circumstances do.
Then Paul reaches the magnificent conclusion of Romans 8.
Romans 8:38–39:
“For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come,
Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.” (KJV).
Look at those words.
Death.
Life.
Things present.
Things to come.
Paul leaves no room for the fear that some created power might become greater than God's saving love in Christ.
And the phrase “I am persuaded” is deeply personal.
Paul was convinced.
Not because he had avoided suffering.
But because he knew the crucified and risen Savior.
And the final words matter:
“In Christ Jesus our Lord.”
This is not a vague promise that everybody is safe regardless of their relationship with God.
Romans 8 begins with the declaration that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
The chapter speaks of the Spirit, adoption, hope, suffering, and God's saving purpose.
Its assurance belongs to those who are united to Christ.
So if you have never surrendered your life to Jesus, do not mistake this message for an invitation to remain unchanged.
It is an invitation to come to Him.
Repent.
Believe the gospel.
Stop defending the sin that is destroying you.
Stop assuming that your good deeds can erase your guilt.
Stop believing that your worst mistake must have the final word.
Turn to the Savior who died and rose again.
And if you already belong to Him but have been living in fear, remember what Paul actually promised.
He did not promise you a world without enemies.
He promised a Savior whose love no enemy can ultimately overcome.
There is a difference.
And that difference can carry a Christian through the darkest night.
I wonder how many people reading this have been silently fighting a battle while everyone around them assumes they are doing fine.
The father who smiles at his children while worrying about how to provide for them.
The mother who prays in the kitchen because she does not want her family to see her crying.
The young believer who is mocked for refusing to compromise.
The person recovering from a sinful past who keeps hearing accusations in their mind.
The widow who still reaches toward the empty side of the bed.
The exhausted Christian who loves Jesus but desperately needs someone to pray with them.
Maybe that person is you.
If it is, please hear this.
You do not have to manufacture a testimony before you are allowed to ask for prayer.
You do not have to pretend your pain is over before you can testify that Christ is faithful.
And you do not have to call your suffering good in order to believe that God is good.
There is room for lament in the Christian life.
There is room for honest prayer.
There is room for tears.
But there is also a hope that refuses to surrender the final word to death.
Because Jesus is risen.
And those who belong to Him have a future that suffering cannot erase.
If this message has touched a place you rarely talk about, I want to invite you to do something more meaningful than simply leaving a reaction.
You do not have to explain everything publicly.
You do not have to expose private wounds to strangers.
But perhaps your honest words will remind another struggling believer that they are not the only one trying to remain faithful through tears.
Not to glorify suffering.
But to glorify the Savior who remained faithful through it.
Somebody reading may need to hear that today.
And please, do not let this message end with you.
They need Romans 8 in its fullness.
They need the cross.
They need the resurrection.
They need the truth that Jesus Christ is not a guarantee of worldly comfort, but the Savior who gives eternal hope.
And if someone comes to mind whose pain should not be exposed publicly, send this privately with compassion instead.
Because there may come a night when you need to read these words again.
God being for you never meant that nothing would come against you. It means that nothing can ultimately overthrow His saving purpose in Christ.
And there is something else I want to share with you.
Gospel Warrior exists to keep bringing people back to Jesus Christ through Scripture-centered teaching, repentance, grace, biblical encouragement, and practical discipleship.
Not every person who encounters our content is standing in a church.
Some are reading alone in bedrooms.
Some are working far from their families.
Some are struggling with doubt.
Some have wandered from the faith.
Some are not believers yet, but they are beginning to ask serious questions about Jesus.
And some are desperately looking for truth in a world filled with noise.
That is why we keep writing, teaching, sharing, and pointing people toward the gospel.
It is not a purchase of spiritual favor.
It is not a substitute for repentance, faith, obedience, or belonging to a local church.
And it should never replace the responsibilities you have toward your family or the faithful stewardship of your resources.
But it can become a voluntary monthly ministry offering, a practical expression of generosity that helps sustain and expand this work.

Scripture teaches that those who proclaim the gospel may receive material support for their work (1 Corinthians 9:14), and that those who are taught the word should share good things with those who teach (Galatians 6:6).
Paul also speaks of generosity as an act of worship and thanksgiving to God in 2 Corinthians 9.
But he is equally clear that giving must not be forced.
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” (2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV).
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not through guilt.
Not through fear.
But through a sincere opportunity to help carry biblical teaching to more people.
These items are simply expressions of appreciation. They do not make anyone more spiritual, and purchasing them is never a measure of devotion to Christ.
It is the opportunity to help make biblical truth more accessible.
We want believers to grow deeper in Jesus Christ, not merely collect inspirational quotes.
We want people to open their Bibles.
To understand the gospel.
To recognize false teaching.
To grow in prayer.
To pursue holiness.
To love their neighbors.
To serve faithfully in their local churches.
And to become more like Christ.
You can pray for this ministry.
You can share its articles.
You can tell a friend about the free resources.
You can help someone encounter Scripture who might otherwise never have opened a Bible.
Your generosity may take different forms, and no one should be made to feel spiritually inferior because of financial limitations.
But remember, the ultimate goal is not to build a large audience around a ministry name.
It is to point people toward the name above every name: Jesus Christ.
Because one day, the articles will stop appearing on our screens.
The comments will grow quiet.
The things we purchased will wear out.
The attention of the world will move somewhere else.
But the Word of God will remain.
And the resurrection of Jesus Christ will still be the foundation of Christian hope.
“If God is for us, who can be against us?”
Paul knew that people could be against us.
He knew governments could oppose believers.
He knew persecutors could imprison them.
He knew hunger could weaken them.
He knew danger could surround them.
He knew swords could kill them.
He did not deny any of it.
He looked directly at those realities and declared that none of them could separate God's people from His love in Christ Jesus.
That is not shallow optimism.
That is resurrection hope.
And perhaps the most beautiful thing about Paul's testimony is that the man who wrote those words was once the enemy.
The persecutor became the preacher.
The guilty man received mercy.
The religious zealot who had opposed Jesus became a servant of Jesus.
The man who had helped spread fear became a messenger of hope.
His past did not become innocent.
His sins did not become harmless.
But his story did not end where his guilt began.
Jesus met him.
Jesus confronted him.
Jesus showed him mercy.
And Jesus changed the direction of his life.
That is grace.
Not grace that ignores sin.
Grace that brings sinners to repentance and makes new life possible through Christ.
And if Jesus could transform Saul the persecutor into Paul the apostle, do not imagine that your life is beyond the reach of His mercy.
Come to Him.
Bring the truth about your sin.
Bring the grief you cannot explain.
Bring the questions you have been afraid to ask.
Bring the weakness you have been trying to hide.
You do not need to impress the Savior.
You need to trust Him.
And if you already belong to Christ, keep looking to Him even when you cannot understand what is happening around you.
His promise is not that you will never walk through the valley.
His promise is greater than that.
For those who are in Christ Jesus, even the valley cannot separate them from His love.

And when everything you thought would protect you has failed, when the world has turned against you, when your strength has reached its limit, and when you have nothing left to boast about except the mercy of Jesus Christ, remember this:
The cross looked like the moment darkness had won—until the empty tomb revealed that darkness never had the final word.
